evidence.body:
# Research brief

## Summary

The EU AI Act (Regulation 2024/1689) entered into force on 1 August 2024 and applies in stages. A SaaS company that only calls third-party AI APIs is usually a deployer, not a provider, so its duties are lighter than those of model vendors. For a small company the practical work is an inventory of where AI is used, a short internal policy, and a record of which provider supplies each model, so that questions from customers and auditors can be answered quickly.

## Key findings

- Timeline: obligations for providers of general-purpose AI models apply from 2 August 2025, twelve months after entry into force. Prohibited practices were banned from 2 February 2025, and most high-risk rules apply from 2 August 2026.

- Penalties: the maximum fine is EUR 35 million or 7% of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher, for prohibited AI practices. Other breaches can reach EUR 15 million or 3%, and supplying incorrect information EUR 7.5 million or 1%. SMEs pay the lower of the two amounts.

- Deployer duties: a company using third-party models must ensure AI literacy of staff (Article 4), meet transparency duties such as telling users they are interacting with a chatbot and labelling AI-generated content (Article 50), and, only if the use case is high-risk, follow the provider's instructions, keep logs and assign human oversight.

## Sources
1. Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Official Journal: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj
2. European Commission, AI Act overview and timeline: https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/regulatory-framework-ai
3. AI Act Explorer, Article 99 (penalties): https://artificialintelligenceact.eu/article/99/

# Research brief

## Summary

This brief summarises what the AI Act means for a small software business that buys AI capabilities from vendors through APIs. For a small company the practical work is an inventory of where AI is used, a short internal policy, and a record of which provider supplies each model, so that questions from customers and auditors can be answered quickly. The company is a deployer under the regulation.

## Key findings

General-purpose AI model rules took effect on 2 August 2025; providers of such models must publish training-data summaries and technical documentation from that date.

Fines are tiered. The top tier is up to 35 million euros or 7 percent of global turnover for banned practices; lower tiers are 15 million or 3 percent and 7.5 million or 1 percent.

As a deployer of external APIs the company's obligations are mainly AI literacy training for staff, transparency notices to end users when they talk to an AI system or see synthetic content, and extra duties only if the product falls into a high-risk category such as hiring or credit scoring.

## Sources
1. Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Official Journal: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj
2. European Commission, AI Act overview and timeline: https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/regulatory-framework-ai
3. AI Act Explorer, Article 99 (penalties): https://artificialintelligenceact.eu/article/99/

# Research brief

## Summary

Short answer: GPAI obligations started in August 2025, fines can reach 7% of turnover, and an API-only SaaS company mostly has transparency and AI-literacy duties. For a small company the practical work is an inventory of where AI is used, a short internal policy, and a record of which provider supplies each model, so that questions from customers and auditors can be answered quickly.

## Key findings

1. When: the general-purpose AI chapter applies from 2 August 2025. Models already on the market before that date have until 2 August 2027 to comply.

2. How much: Article 99 sets maximum administrative fines of EUR 35m or 7% of total worldwide annual turnover for prohibited practices, and EUR 15m or 3% for most other violations.

3. What we must do: because we integrate third-party models rather than build them, we are a deployer. We must make sure staff have sufficient AI literacy, disclose AI interactions and AI-generated content to users, and check whether any feature is high-risk under Annex III, which would add human oversight and logging duties.

## Sources
1. Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Official Journal: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj
2. European Commission, AI Act overview and timeline: https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/regulatory-framework-ai

# Research brief

## Summary

SOC 2 is an attestation report defined by the AICPA. For a 20-person startup the main decision is whether to start with a Type I or go straight to a Type II report. For a twenty-person team the practical work is choosing an auditor early, adopting a compliance automation tool or a spreadsheet control matrix, and assigning one owner for evidence collection so the audit window is not wasted.

## Key findings

- Type I vs Type II: a Type I report assesses whether controls are suitably designed at a single point in time, while a Type II report tests whether those controls actually operated effectively over a period of time.

- Observation period: a Type II audit covers an observation window that is typically between three and twelve months; many first-time audits use a three-month or six-month window.

- Cost: for a small startup the auditor's fee for a Type II report is commonly in the range of USD 12,000 to 40,000, plus compliance software and internal staff time, so total first-year cost often lands between 30,000 and 80,000 dollars.

## Sources
1. AICPA, SOC 2 overview: https://www.aicpa-cima.com/topic/audit-assurance/audit-and-assurance-greater-than-soc-2
2. Vanta, SOC 2 Type I vs Type II: https://www.vanta.com/collection/soc-2/soc-2-type-1-vs-type-2
3. Drata, How much does a SOC 2 audit cost: https://drata.com/grc-central/soc-2/cost

# Research brief

## Summary

Customers asking for SOC 2 usually want a Type II report. This brief explains the two report types, how long the audit window lasts and what it costs. For a twenty-person team the practical work is choosing an auditor early, adopting a compliance automation tool or a spreadsheet control matrix, and assigning one owner for evidence collection so the audit window is not wasted.

## Key findings

The difference: Type I is a snapshot of control design on one date; Type II proves the controls worked consistently across a review window, which is why enterprise buyers prefer it.

The observation period for Type II is usually 3 to 12 months, with 6 months being a common choice for a first report.

Typical spend for a startup: audit fees of roughly $15k to $40k for Type II, and $5k to $25k per year for automation tooling, before counting engineering time.

The audit window usually runs six months for a first report, and can be anywhere from 3 to 12 months.

Budget roughly $20,000 to $35,000 in auditor fees for a small company, plus tooling.
